incidents.title: ruflo MCP bridge: unauthenticated remote code execution in default Docker Compose setup
incidents.evidenceQuote: The docker-compose defaults bound the bridge and MongoDB to all interfaces.
incidents.attackSurface: Local AI dev tools / MCP server
incidents.tldrRootCause: The default compose file exposed an unauthenticated MCP endpoint and MongoDB on all network interfaces, allowing remote command execution.
incidents.realisticRootCause: POST /mcp had no authentication and bypassed the blocklist for terminal_execute, giving a shell in the bridge container and access to every provider API key in its environment. An attacker could also write poisoned patterns into the AgentDB store, which a patched redeploy does not remove.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Only if you or your team run ruflo from its Docker Compose file; look for ports 3001 and 27017 listening beyond localhost.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A ruflo stack started with the defaults on a laptop or cloud VM would let anyone on the same network, or the internet if the ports are open, run commands and read your AI provider keys.
lockItDown: Search your projects and running containers for ruflo; if present, confirm ports 3001 and 27017 are bound to loopback only and update to the fixed release.
If an instance was ever network-reachable, rotate the OpenAI, Google, OpenRouter and Anthropic keys it held and audit the AgentDB pattern store for injected entries.
incidents.roleAngle: A clear example of AI agent tooling shipping with unauthenticated tool execution bound to all interfaces by default.

incidents.title: Remus infostealer reads Gmail through a fake Google Sheets Chrome extension
incidents.evidenceQuote: The Remus infostealer is stealing Gmail messages through a stealthy malicious Chrome extension
incidents.tldrRootCause: The Remus infostealer, once on a machine, uses a malicious Chrome extension posing as Google Sheets to read Gmail messages.
incidents.realisticRootCause: The extension works inside the signed-in browser session, so it reads mail without needing the password or MFA. How Remus first reaches the endpoint is not stated in the evidence.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, if an infostealer lands on a laptop where you use Chrome with Gmail; look for a Google Sheets extension you did not install.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: An infostealer infection on your Mac or Windows laptop could add the extension to Chrome, which then reads mail from your logged-in Gmail session.
lockItDown: Open chrome://extensions in each Chrome profile and remove any Google Sheets-branded or unfamiliar extension you did not install, especially ones loaded outside the Chrome Web Store.
Open chrome://management and confirm the browser is managed only by your organisation; where you administer Chrome, restrict installs to an extension allowlist.
incidents.roleAngle: A browser extension inherits the user's session, so it defeats MFA; an extension allowlist is the control that matters here.

incidents.roleAngle: A managed cloud service was the exposure point, so secrets kept in platform configuration need the same rotation plan as secrets in code.

incidents.title: PolinRider campaign plants malware in over 7,600 GitHub repositories owned by real developers
incidents.tldrRootCause: Not stated; since the repos belong to real developers, attackers likely pushed with stolen developer credentials or tokens.

incidents.evidenceQuote: use of voice phishing (aka vishing) attacks to trick targets into entering credentials in phishing pages

Review which cloud services are reachable from the internet and compare against the network and system indicators in Microsoft's ARTEX post.
incidents.roleAngle: Automated secret hunting shortens the time between a leaked key and its abuse, so rotation speed matters more than detection alone.

incidents.title: Reporter with no bug-hunting experience finds WordPress plugin CSRF with free AI models
incidents.tldrRootCause: Not an incident: a first-person account of finding a CSRF bug (CVE-2026-124251) in a WordPress plugin using two free LLMs.
incidents.realisticRootCause: The piece describes discovering and reporting a cross-site request forgery flaw in a plugin with over 40,000 installs in six hours. The plugin is not named in the excerpt and no exploitation is described.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Not directly; WordPress is outside your footprint and the plugin is not named in the evidence.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: There is no direct path; the relevance is the trend that low-skill, AI-assisted bug discovery is now practical.
incidents.roleAngle: Evidence that the skill barrier for finding common bug classes is dropping, which shortens the realistic window between code release and bug reports.
